item.title: Single- and Two-Qubit Gates Driven by an Integrated Photonic Laser
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Single-qubit average Clifford fidelity reaches 99.61%±0.03% and two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen Bell-state fidelity reaches 92.35%±1.50% using a chip-scale Brillouin laser locked to an integrated coil resonator.

Grade 0.475 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Chris Caron, Zhenyu Wei, Andrei Isichenko, David Heim, Meiting Song, Nick Montifiore, Kaikai Liu, Josiah Dill, Daniel J. Blumenthal, Robert J. Niffenegger

Figure

Resolved sideband cooling, Rabi oscillations, and randomized benchmarking curve showing sequence survival fidelity as a function of Clifford gate depth d.

Asks

Can an integrated visible-wavelength narrow-linewidth photonic laser meet the phase-noise and coherence requirements to drive coherent single- and two-qubit gates on trapped-ion optical qubits?

But

Coherence limited by residual laser drift and AC mains magnetic-field fluctuations; separate chips connected via fibers/free-space optics rather than full monolithic integration.

Tools

integrated Si₃N₄ Brillouin laser · integrated coil resonator reference · surface electrode trap with ⁸⁸Sr⁺ ions · active fiber noise cancellation · adaptive Bayesian fluorescence detection

Abstract

Trapped ions are a leading technology for quantum computing, but their reliance on bespoke tabletop laser and optical systems remains a major obstacle to scaling and robustness. Integrated silicon nitride lasers, compatible with future monolithic integration with surface electrode ion traps, have recently demonstrated frequency-selective qubit state preparation and measurement as well as interrogation of an optical clock transition. However, coherent qubit gates driven by integrated laser sources have not yet been demonstrated because coherent quantum logic imposes substantially more stringent performance requirements on the laser. Here, we use a visible-wavelength integrated Brillouin laser stabilized to an integrated coil resonator to drive coherent single- and two-qubit gates with ⁸⁸Sr⁺ optical qubits. We measure an average single-qubit fidelity of 99.61% ± 0.03% per Clifford gate with randomized benchmarking and use a two-qubit Mølmer-Sørensen interaction to generate an entangled Bell state with a fidelity of 92.35% ± 1.50%. The qubit exhibits a bare Ramsey coherence time of 660 ± 9 μs, extended to 1.750 ± 0.033 ms by spin echo. These results demonstrate that integrated visible-wavelength narrow-linewidth photonic lasers can meet the phase-noise requirements for coherent trapped ion quantum logic, providing a path for scalable optical systems integrated within trapped ion quantum processors.

item.title: Telecom-Integrated Photonic Memory Operating Near the Mechanical Ground State
item.description:
Worth a look new result — On-chip absorptive optomechanical memory stores telecom-band photons with on-demand retrieval at mechanical phonon occupancy of 0.32.

Grade 0.471 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “cavity QED, atom-photon interfaces and quantum networks” · Jindao Tang, Bo Jing, Liping Zeng, Peiqin Chen, Hengrui Liang, Yifei Zhang, Xinyao Xu, Qizhi Cai, Xueying Zhang, Qiang Zhou, You Wang, Haizhi Song, Guangcan Guo, Guangwei Deng

Asks

Can an on-chip, telecom-compatible optomechanical memory operate near its mechanical ground state with on-demand retrieval for few-photon inputs?

But

Operated in a dilution refrigerator at 20 mK under tailored control field pulses to suppress optical heating; demonstrated at few-photon input levels.

Tools

Optomechanically induced transparency (OMIT) · Nanofabricated mechanical resonator · Dilution refrigerator at 20 mK · Pulsed control field engineering

Abstract

Scalable quantum networks require quantum memories that are chip-integrated, telecom-band compatible, and capable of flexible retrieval. Nanofabricated mechanical resonators meet these criteria. They offer independent tunability of optical and mechanical modes, long-lived phonon states, and design flexibility beyond atomic systems, making them strong candidates for practical integrated quantum memory. Here, we demonstrate an on-chip, absorptive optomechanical memory for telecom-band photons, based on optomechanically induced transparency (OMIT) and operating near the mechanical ground state. The device stores telecom-band photons, demonstrating compatibility with external photon sources at the few-photon level, while enabling on-demand retrieval. By placing the device in a dilution refrigerator at 20 mK and tailoring the control field to suppress optical heating, we achieve a remarkably low phonon occupancy of just 0.32 during the storage process. Our results lay the groundwork for scalable, phonon-based quantum memory devices and open new avenues for integrating mechanical systems into practical quantum network architectures.

item.title: From Bits to Qubits: The Theory and Practice of Quantum Data Encoding
item.description:
Worth a look review — Surveys quantum data encoding methods across state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM, and block-encoding, synthesizing circuit size, depth, and fault-tolerant gate counts.

Grade 0.457 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Xiao-Ming Zhang, Arthur G. Rattew, Bujiao Wu, Georgios Styliaris, Xiaoming Sun, Bálint Koczor, Xiao Yuan

Figure

Three core access models mapping classical vectors and matrices to quantum operations: quantum state preparation, QRAM, and block-encoding.

Asks

How can deterministic classical data be compiled into quantum representations under minimal circuit depth, gate counts, and non-Clifford resources?

But

Restricted to deterministic, fully known classical data in the standard qubit circuit model with all-to-all or binary-tree connectivity; excludes sampled distributions and continuous variables.

Tools

uniformly controlled rotations (UCR) · Schmidt decomposition · QRAM bucket-brigade architecture · linear combination of unitaries (LCU) · block-encoding

Abstract

Encoding classical data into quantum systems is a foundational step in the execution of nearly all quantum algorithms, and a critical bottleneck in realizing practical quantum advantage. This review provides a comprehensive account of the concepts, algorithms, and practical considerations associated with quantum data encoding. We trace the development from its early conceptual foundations to recent advances, considering commonly used access models, such as quantum state preparation, unitary synthesis, QRAM and block encoding. We survey the circuit size, depth, space-time tradeoffs, as well as non-Clifford resources required for fault-tolerant implementation. We also discuss the roles of different access models in quantum algorithms. Special attention is given to structured data, such as sparse data, Boolean functions and data represented by tensor networks. This review bridges theory and applications, serving both as a pedagogical guide for newcomers and as a reference for active researchers. We also highlight the pivotal role of quantum data encoding in quantum computing and provide insights into future directions that will enable quantum advantage.

item.title: Dynamics of entanglement in non-Hermitian system of nonreciprocal coupling
item.description:
Worth a look theory — Non-reciprocal three-cavity system exhibits a third-order exceptional point from the coalescence of two second-order exceptional points, speeding up entanglement generation time to tm≈15 ns with an enhancement factor scaling as J−4/5.

Grade 0.455 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Jiguo Wu, Shaojie Yang, Xiong Liu, Zhibo Jiang, Zhiyou Zhang, Rongchun Ge

Figure

Phase diagram over asymmetry parameter e and coupling Ω2, showing boundaries for second-order exceptional points (extEP2) and third-order exceptional points (extEP3) separating symmetry-unbroken and broken phases.

Asks

How do interactions between different orders of exceptional points affect entanglement dynamics and generation speed in non-reciprocally coupled quantum systems?

Before

Hermitian counterpart required tm≈250 ns to reach maximum entanglement generation time.

But

Single-excitation subspace under post-selection against decay to ground state |0,0,0⟩; assumes cavity dissipation rates are matched (Δγ/γ≪1).

Tools

non-Hermitian PT-symmetric Hamiltonian · concurrence and entanglement entropy · quantum fidelity metric · gauged semiconductor laser array mapping

Abstract

The exploration of the effect of non-Hermitian (NH) in quantum systems is gaining renewed momentum as a result of the recent progress in experiments. It has been indicated that the ability to engineer the orders of exceptional points (EPs) can be fundamental to its applications in quantum control, such as accelerating entanglement generation; however, an initial survey of the interactions between different orders of EPs is still missing. In this work, we try to partially address this issue by employing a non-reciprocally coupled cavity system which can be experimentally realizable with a two-dimensional reconfigurable NH gauged laser array. With deliberate design, our systems display both second and third orders of EPs. The sign of a novel, purely quantum continuous entanglement phase transition is observed, which reveals how multi-EP interactions alter entanglement dynamics across different regimes while maintaining accelerated generation. Our findings reveil the genuinely quantum NH physics of higher-order EPs, which has opened up a new avenue for future investigations of the higher-order degeneracy application and the dynamic phase transitions of quantum systems.

item.title: Propaq: A Python package for Heisenberg Propagation
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Rust-backed Python library Propaq matches monoprop and achieves up to ∼100× speedup over existing packages like pauli-prop, pyrauli, and PauliPropagation.jl at 109 terms. Natively supports arbitrary operator bases and hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation.

Grade 0.454 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Hrishikesh Belagali, Ryan LaRose

Figure

Propagation wall time in seconds (main plot) and number of terms (inset) versus Trotter step count for TFIM (left) and Hubbard (right) models across multiple propagation packages using 64 threads and a 10−6 coefficient cutoff.

Asks

How to implement a flexible, high-performance Heisenberg propagation package supporting arbitrary operator bases and hybrid simulation schemes?

Before

Packages including pauli-prop, pyrauli, PauliPropagation.jl, and MajoranaPropagation.jl.

But

Coefficient truncation threshold of 10−6; benchmarks evaluated on 64 AMD EPYC 7H12 cores for Trotterized 2D TFIM and 2D Hubbard models.

Tools

Rust core with Python bindings · Heisenberg propagation (Pauli, Majorana, Weyl-Heisenberg) · Matrix product state Schrödinger simulation · Multi-threaded CPU parallelization

Abstract

We introduce Propaq, a performant and flexible Python package implementing Heisenberg propagation techniques for classically simulating quantum circuits. Propaq is compatible with major quantum software packages like Qiskit and Cirq, and matches or outperforms similar state-of-the-art packages for Heisenberg propagation. Beyond this, Propaq has multiple distinguishing features for simulation and research. These include Heisenberg propagation in any basis, hybrid Schrödinger-Heisenberg simulation, custom truncation and noisy simulation methods, and detailed logging information for analyzing simulation accuracy, runtime, and memory usage. We describe these features, how to use Propaq for research, and its backend implementation.

item.title: Quantum magnonics with engineered dissipative and coherent interactions
item.description:
Worth a look review — Cavity magnonics can be driven into non-Hermitian and quantum regimes via reservoir-mediated dissipative coupling, Floquet frequency modulation, and parametric squeezing transfer. Long-lived subradiant modes near anti-𝒫𝒯 exceptional points lower the bistability threshold as |Ωth|2∝(γ−Γ)3/K, scaling quantum Fisher information as ℱQ∝ε−4.

Grade 0.454 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Debsuvra Mukhopadhyay, Jayakrishnan M. P. Nair, Girish S. Agarwal

Figure

Real and imaginary eigenspectrum parts plotted versus relative detuning δ. At exceptional points |δ|=Γ, real frequencies coalesce while imaginary damping rates bifurcate into superradiant and subradiant branches.

Asks

How do engineered dissipative coupling, Floquet modulation, and parametric driving enable quantum state generation, nonreciprocal transport, and enhanced sensing in cavity magnonics?

But

Dynamical stability requires parametric drive strength x<1. Bright-magnon quadrature squeezing persists only below critical thermal occupation n‾mcrit.

Tools

bad-cavity adiabatic elimination · anti-PT symmetry engineering · Floquet sideband modulation · cavity parametric driving · quantum Langevin equations

Abstract

Cavity magnonics is moving beyond the conventional paradigm of coherent spin--photon hybridization toward the controlled engineering of dissipative and coherent interactions, Floquet dynamics, and quantum fluctuations. This Perspective examines how these ingredients reshape collective dynamics and open new avenues for quantum state engineering, transport, and sensing. We discuss the role of dissipative coupling and anti-PT symmetry in enabling long-lived collective modes and enhanced spectral response, and highlight Floquet engineering as a means of engineering nonreciprocal transport and phase-controlled interactions. We then review recent progress in quantum magnonics, ranging from squeezed and entangled magnon states, including the squeezing of thermal magnons, to prospective schemes for preparing magnonic Schrödinger-cat states. We also discuss how parametric driving and active gain strongly modify hybrid susceptibilities and amplify magnon--photon response. These advances expand the scope of cavity magnonics beyond conventional polariton physics, establishing it as a versatile platform for sensing, transduction, spin transport, and hybrid quantum technologies.

item.title: Single-tone drive-enhanced CROT gate for bosonic quantum error correction
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Amplifies cross-Kerr interaction between two microwave cavity modes via single-frequency transmon drive near intermediate-state divergences, achieving on-demand ᴄʀᴏᴛ gate for rotation-symmetric bosonic error correction without requiring multiple frequencies or frequency-tunable elements.

Grade 0.451 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum information with Rydberg atoms” · Shushen Qin, Long D. H. My, Adrian Copetudo, Amon M. Kasper, Yvonne Y. Gao, Hui Khoon Ng

Figure

Effective self- and cross-Kerr nonlinearities plotted against drive detuning at fixed drive strength |Ωd/δd|=1, showing resonant divergences that enhance cross-Kerr interaction while distinguishing two-cavity from single-cavity resonances.

Asks

How can a direct, code-agnostic ᴄʀᴏᴛ gate between bosonic cavity modes be implemented in circuit QED without multi-tone driving or gigahertz frequency tuning?

Before

Prior direct implementations required >1 GHz frequency tunability or multi-tone drives scaling with logical state size.

But

Numerical and analytical modeling. Assumes perfect cancellation of self-Kerr from auxiliary side transmons, neglecting higher-order mode distortions and unmodeled side-transmon Hilbert spaces.

Tools

circuit QED · transmon-mediated cross-Kerr enhancement · fourth-order perturbation theory · side-transmon self-Kerr cancellation · teleportation-based bosonic error correction

Abstract

Bosonic error correction provides a hardware-efficient route to protected qubits for accurate quantum information processing. A critical component for error correction of rotation-symmetric bosonic (RSB) codes, like the well-known cat codes, is the two-mode controlled-rotation (CROT) operation. The CROT gate is useful because of its code-agnostic generality and its error-propagation properties. While the CROT gate can in principle be composed from existing bosonic physical primitives, the desirable properties are typically lost when composed as a sequence of imperfect primitive operations. Past work has focused on direct implementations that rely on features of specific codes. Here, we present a direct route to CROT within the circuit-QED architecture that retains its code-agnostic and error-propagation characteristics. By driving a transmon simultaneously coupled to two microwave cavities, we controllably enhance the effective nonlinearities between the microwave cavities and thus engineer the necessary two-mode interaction underlying the CROT gate. Using only a single drive frequency, we can achieve an on-off ratio sufficient for gate implementation, while minimizing mode distortions. We provide simple analytical formulas that permit the identification of potential working regimes, further refined by exact numerics, and illustrate the efficacy of our CROT approach in an error-correction example involving different RSB codes within the same circuit. Our CROT gate adds to the arsenal of direct two-mode gates available for general bosonic information processing.

item.arxave:abstract: Bosonic error correction provides a hardware-efficient route to protected qubits for accurate quantum information processing. A critical component for error correction of rotation-symmetric bosonic (RSB) codes, like the well-known cat codes, is the two-mode controlled-rotation (CROT) operation. The CROT gate is useful because of its code-agnostic generality and its error-propagation properties. While the CROT gate can in principle be composed from existing bosonic physical primitives, the desirable properties are typically lost when composed as a sequence of imperfect primitive operations. Past work has focused on direct implementations that rely on features of specific codes. Here, we present a direct route to CROT within the circuit-QED architecture that retains its code-agnostic and error-propagation characteristics. By driving a transmon simultaneously coupled to two microwave cavities, we controllably enhance the effective nonlinearities between the microwave cavities and thus engineer the necessary two-mode interaction underlying the CROT gate. Using only a single drive frequency, we can achieve an on-off ratio sufficient for gate implementation, while minimizing mode distortions. We provide simple analytical formulas that permit the identification of potential working regimes, further refined by exact numerics, and illustrate the efficacy of our CROT approach in an error-correction example involving different RSB codes within the same circuit. Our CROT gate adds to the arsenal of direct two-mode gates available for general bosonic information processing.

item.title: Matrix Holography on an Optical Lattice
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Constructs bosonic four-body matrix-quantum-mechanics potentials via Floquet-engineered oscillating two-body spin interactions with a constant number of unitaries per cycle. Control-frequency bandwidth scales as 𝒪(N3) with matrix size N, reaching non-perturbative couplings λ∼𝒪(1) at driving frequencies ω∼𝒪(MHz).

Grade 0.439 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “photonic qubits, linear-optical computing and boson sampling” · Robin Löwenberg, Julian Sonner

Figure

Ground-state energy convergence as a function of spin size j comparing the large-spin model against the truncated SU(2)×SO(2) bosonic matrix model with λ=2 and cutoff Λ=6. Relative error is 0.5% at j=3 and drops to 0.007%.

Asks

Can four-body potentials of bosonic matrix quantum mechanics be simulated on an analog optical-lattice platform without the deep circuits of digital implementations?

But

Requires non-spin-conserving spin-spin interactions and large-spin ferromagnetic regime (m∼j). Bosonic Hilbert space must be truncated.

Tools

Holstein-Primakoff transformation · Floquet engineering · Magnus expansion · James' effective Hamiltonian method · optical lattice of atomic ensembles

Abstract

We propose an analog quantum-simulation protocol based on a lattice of atomic ensembles and time-averaged Floquet dynamics to construct the four-body potentials that typically appear in bosonic BFSS-like matrix quantum mechanics. In contrast to gate-based digital implementations requiring deep circuits, our approach generates the target model through a fixed set of control stages per Floquet cycle, keeping the number of consecutive unitaries constant with respect to the matrix size N. The principal scaling cost in our construction is given by the frequency range required to control the growing lattice. We show that this cost grows at most as O(N³), giving a polynomial scaling route to large-N, attractive to experimental implementation. Additionally, we demonstrate that the coupling parameter can be tuned beyond O(1), enabling the simulation of strong-coupling physics necessary for holographic phases.
